title: Garland
subtitle: A chain of atolls strung across the equator

chapters.label: CHAPTER 01 · ATOLL REACH
chapters.heading: A line of islands against the sky.
chapters.subheading: Twenty-six atolls stretch across the equator.
chapters.body: The Maldives lie in the Indian Ocean, southwest of India and Sri Lanka, about seven hundred fifty kilometres from the mainland. Their chain of twenty-six atolls extends from Ihavandhippolhu in the north to Addu in the south, crossing the equator.

chapters.label: CHAPTER 02 · NAME'S THREAD
chapters.heading: Words woven from sand and sea.
chapters.subheading: Etymology ties islands to a necklace.
chapters.body: Legends say the first settlers were the Dheyvis, and the kingdom was known as Dheeva Maari. Scholars link the name Maldives to Sanskrit mālā meaning garland and dvīpa meaning island, a translation echoed in Sinhala as Maala Divaina, Tamil as mālaittīvu, and Malayalam as māladvīpŭ. The term evokes a necklace of islands.

chapters.label: CHAPTER 03 · ANCIENT WAVES
chapters.heading: Stories carved in coral and copper.
chapters.body: Archaeological evidence suggests kingdoms existed in the fifth to sixth century BCE, and oral tradition records migrations from the southern Indian subcontinent. Artefacts show the presence of Hinduism before the Islamic period. Ibn Battuta called the islands Maḥal Dībīyāt, using the Arabic word for palace.
